answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Genuinely Keats. The line opens the second stanza of “Ode on a Grecian Urn,” first published in January 1820. The primary text reads “Heard melodies are sweet, but those unheard / Are sweeter” — the popular one-line form simply joins the two verse lines, and the wording is faithful.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: January 1820, in Annals of the Fine Arts; collected the same year in Lamia, Isabella, The Eve of St. Agnes, and Other Poems

source.excerpt:
Heard melodies are sweet, but those unheard
Are sweeter; therefore, ye soft pipes, play on;
Not to the sensual ear, but, more endear’d,
Pipe to the spirit ditties of no tone…
trail: The line opens the second stanza of Keats’s “Ode on a Grecian Urn” ↗, written May 1819.
It first reached print in January 1820, and was collected that year in Keats’s Lamia… volume — see the 1820 text on Wikisource ↗.
The primary text reads “Heard melodies are sweet, but those unheard / Are sweeter”, confirmed against Wikipedia’s account of the poem ↗.
source.excerptNote: The famous one-line quotation collapses the first two verse lines into a single sentence; the wording is Keats’s own.

author.name: John Keats
author.heading: About the author
author.bio: John Keats was a leading poet of the second generation of English Romantics, celebrated for his sensuous imagery and his “Great Odes” of 1819. “Ode on a Grecian Urn” — source of both this line and “Beauty is truth, truth beauty” — is among the most quoted poems in English. He died of tuberculosis in Rome at just 25.

context.heading: Why it matters
lead: Keats’s paradox — that imagined music outdoes anything the ear can catch — grew out of contemplating the silent figures on an ancient urn. The pipers carved on it will never sound a note, yet precisely because they are frozen and unheard, the melody the viewer imagines is “sweeter.”
The line has become shorthand for the Romantic conviction that the imagination surpasses mere sensation, and it is quoted far beyond poetry — in essays on art, music, and desire.
